entry.title: Abstractions for scaling reinforcement learning in JAX

link.title: Abstractions for scaling reinforcement learning in JAX

entry.content:
In Behavioral Language Modeling I argued that a language model acting as an agent is a recurrent policy in a POMDP, and that a recurrent RL algorithm can train it whether a GRU or a language model processes the history. This post is about the library where that holds in code. It is called boonta, after the podrace Anakin wins in The Phantom Menace, and it is built around one idea. The algorithm, the environment and the training loop should never meet. If they never meet, then a GRU learning CartPole from scratch and a pretrained Qwen3 playing Wordle through tool calls are the same program with different parts plugged in, and everything the RL community has built for partially observable problems applies to the LLM for free.

The same holds along the whole training pipeline and across modalities. Next-token pre-training is behaviour cloning, so it runs through the same algorithm interface as RL post-training, with the same network and checkpoints. And a vision-language-action model such as π0 is just another policy, one that reads camera frames and emits robot actions.

Most of what follows is about where the boundaries sit and why. The LLM shows up near the end, and by then there is almost nothing left to say about it, which is the point.

Three things that never meet

boonta has three kinds of object, and each one owns exactly one thing.

  1. The algorithm decides what to do and learns from what happened. It never touches the environment or the devices.
  2. The environment is the game. It never knows who is playing it.
  3. The podracer is the training loop. It owns the devices and the sharding, and calls the other two. It never knows what either of them is doing.

The only place they meet is a recipe, one plain file per algorithm and suite that builds an environment, a network, an optimizer and an algorithm and hands them to a podracer. There is no shared helper layer between recipes. Each one reads top to bottom on its own, and copying the closest one is how you start a new one.

This sounds like ordinary modularity, and most RL libraries claim it. The test is what each interface is allowed to see, and the rest of the post is mostly about those signatures.

The algorithm sees three calls

An algorithm is three pure functions, and all three run inside jax.jit.

Method Called Returns
init(key, timestep) once, with the first timestep the algorithm state
step(state, key, timestep, temperature) every environment step (state, action, aux)
update(state, key, transitions) once per batch the new state

The network and the optimizer are passed in, never built inside, so the same PPO runs a CNN on MinAtar and an MLP on CartPole. And there is no policy object. The network’s head returns a distribution, so the network is the policy and step simply samples from what it returns. Temperature goes to the head and nowhere else, which is how one flag makes evaluation greedy for a categorical policy, ε-greedy for a Q-network and tighter for a Gaussian.

The decision I care most about is where the recurrent state lives. It does not live in the algorithm. A recurrent carry is rollout state, exactly like the environment state, so the podracer owns it. A recurrent algorithm’s step takes the carry in and hands it back out, the podracer records the carry that entered every step, and update replays the rollout from the carry it started on. Two things follow. A checkpoint holds only what was learned, never a half-finished episode’s memory. And the algorithm cannot tell what kind of memory it is threading through time, a GRU’s hidden state, a state-space model’s scan or a transformer’s KV cache. That last fact is what the whole LLM story rests on.

The environment sees nothing but actions

Every environment, whether it is pure JAX, a Gymnasium simulator or C++ called through FFI, has the same small interface. init and step return a Timestep carrying the observation, the action that led to it, the reward and two flags, terminated for a real end and truncated for a cut. The distinction matters because a value target bootstraps through a truncation but not through a termination, and conflating the two is one of the quietest bugs in RL.

Two conventions do a lot of work. Episodes reset on the same step they end, so the final reward and the first observation of the next episode arrive together and the loop never pauses. And the first timestep of every episode sets terminated, which is exactly the signal a recurrent network needs to wipe its memory. Every recurrent block resets to a blank carry wherever that flag is set, so episodes can never leak into each other, however the rollout is chunked.

Wrappers are environments around environments, and a podracer always receives a batched, auto-resetting stack. A game with free parameters, such as a Kinetix level, also exposes update(state, key, theta=...), which means “play this theta from its start”. That one method is how curricula reach into the game without the game knowing a curriculum exists.

Three podracers

The training loop is modelled on DeepMind’s Podracer architectures [Hessel et al.], and the three podracers are named after the drivers in the race.

🏎️ Anakin is for environments written in JAX. Acting, stepping and learning compile into a single program, the environments are split across every device on a data mesh axis, and the parameters are replicated. Training is one jax.jit call that scans over updates, each of which scans over environment steps and then calls update. With num_processes set it spans every device of every machine, so going from one GPU to a SLURM allocation is a command-line flag.

🔧 Sebulba is for environments that are slow or not JAX at all. Actor threads step their own environments on some devices while a learner trains on the rest. The lag between them is fixed at exactly one update, as in Cleanba [Huang et al.], so rollout k is always collected with the parameters of update k−2 and a run is reproducible at a fixed seed regardless of thread timing.

📼 Quadinaros is for offline RL and behaviour cloning. It samples batches from a fixed dataset inside a jitted scan and only touches the environment to evaluate.

Sharding is declared, not coded. A field of an algorithm’s state marked metadata={"axis": "data"}, such as a replay buffer with one row per environment, is split across devices along with the environments. Everything unmarked is replicated. So an algorithm never mentions a device, and a podracer never needs to know what a replay buffer is.

Pit and lap

Curricula are where I most wanted the boundaries to hold, because curricula want to touch everything. They read how the agent is doing, rewrite which levels it plays, and in a league even reset the learner. In most codebases that means a curriculum-specific training loop.

In boonta every podracer takes two hooks instead. A pit learns from each rollout after the algorithm’s update and then rewrites the environment, once per update. A lap fires after every single environment step, for state the game must see continuously. Both have their own state, which the podracer carries and shards like anything else.

A curriculum is then just a function that takes an algorithm and an environment and returns an algorithm, an environment, a pit and a lap. Prioritized Level Replay [Jiang et al.] is a pit that scores levels by how much the agent learned from them and replays the most useful ones. Success-rate-targeted sampling is a pit that keeps a fixed pool of tasks and draws them by how close each one’s success rate sits to a target. A league is a pit that seats opponents from a pool of earlier policies, all the way up to PSRO [Lanctot et al.]. None of them needed a change to an algorithm, an environment or a podracer, and all of them run on every podracer. This is also the part of the library I care most about for generalization. Which tasks an agent sees, in what order, and how diverse they are is the lever on whether it learns a skill or memorises a training set, and it should be as easy to swap as an optimizer.

The network is three slots

A Network has a feature extractor, an optional torso and a head.

network = Network(
    feature_extractor=FeatureExtractor(observation_extractor=cnn),
    torso=RNN(GRUCell(256)),  # optional, takes and returns a carry
    head=ActorCritic(actor=Categorical(nn.Dense(num_actions)), critic=nn.Dense(1)),
)

Every torso is a Block whose call takes (carry, x, done) and returns (carry, x). Cells, torsos and stacks are separate config groups, so a GRU in a sequential scan, a MinGRU in a parallel scan, a self-attention block with a KV cache, a highway stack or a Llama-style stack are all one command-line override apart. Mixed precision follows one rule, bf16 for anything that enters a matrix multiply and fp32 for anything accumulated, and distribution parameters and values are always cast back to fp32 before they reach a loss.

The interface is narrow enough that a pretrained transformer is just another Block. Qwen3 and Gemma are implemented as stacks of attention and GLU blocks whose carry is the KV cache, and their HuggingFace weights load straight into them. LoRA wraps any block, keeps the base weights frozen and optionally quantized, and trains only the adapters.

An LLM, plugged in

Here is the Wordle recipe, trimmed to the parts that matter. The game itself is a plain JAX environment that takes a five-letter guess and returns per-letter feedback. Two wrappers turn it into a language game.

env = environments.make(**cfg.environment)               # wordle, in JAX
env = MCP(env, to_action=parse_tool_call, to_tokens=feedback_tokens, ...)
env = Prompt(env, tokenizer.encode(SYSTEM_PROMPT).ids, pad)
env = instantiate(cfg.environment.auto_reset, env)

torso = Chunked(LoRA(block=qwen3, params=quantize(pretrained), rank=8, alpha=16.0))
embed = nn.Embed(vocab_size, hidden, embedding_init=init_fn(embeddings))

network = Network(
    feature_extractor=TokenFeatureExtractor(embed=embed),
    torso=torso,
    head=ActorCritic(actor=Categorical(Unembed(embed=embed)), critic=nn.Dense(1)),
)
algorithm = RecurrentPPO(cfg=..., network=network, optimizer=...)

The MCP wrapper is where tokens become actions. From the algorithm’s side the action space is the vocabulary, and every environment step is one sampled token. The wrapper watches the stream, starts collecting when the model opens a <tool_call>, and when it closes the call it parses the JSON, steps the real game once with the guess, and returns the feedback as observation tokens. On every other step nothing comes back from the world, and the observation is padding. The Prompt wrapper feeds the system prompt in as the first observation of every episode.

So the POMDP from the BLM post is not a metaphor here, it is the data layout. Observations and actions arrive on separate, step-aligned channels. The policy’s tokens are the action channel, the prompt and the game’s feedback are the observation channel, and the reward lands when the game says so. There is no loss mask anywhere in the code, because there is nothing to mask. The KV cache is the carry, the podracer threads it through time exactly as it would a GRU’s hidden state, and the critic reads the same torso and so conditions on the whole history. The action embedding and the actor’s readout are both tied to the model’s own token embeddings, so “tokens are actions” is literal all the way down to the parameters.

Then the payoff. Swap RecurrentPPO for RecurrentGRPO and nothing else changes. Swap Qwen3 for Gemma and nothing else changes. Set num_processes=8 and the same run spans two machines.

Pre-training is behaviour cloning

The same picture covers pre-training, seen from the other side. A corpus is a record of someone else’s actions, and next-token prediction is behaviour cloning on that record. In boonta that is not an analogy either. It is RecurrentBC on Quadinaros, which samples token sequences from a dataset instead of rolling out an environment, and trains the same Network with the same torso, the same sharding and the same checkpoint format as the RL run that follows it.

So a model can go from pre-training to RL post-training without changing libraries, data layouts or model code. The pre-training run and the RL run differ in the algorithm object and the podracer, and in nothing else. It is also the shape of the comparison in the BLM post. Cloning every token and cloning only the agent’s actions are the same algorithm with a different choice of which tokens count as actions.

Vision-language-action models

Nothing above is specific to text. A vision-language-action model is a policy whose observations include camera frames and whose actions are robot commands, and it fits the same three slots. boonta implements π0, with a SigLIP vision encoder, a Gemma language backbone and a separate action expert, and loads its published weights into that structure. On the environment side, LIBERO and Isaac Lab Arena wrap robot manipulation suites behind the usual init and step.

That means a VLA gets the same treatment as the LLM. It can be fine-tuned by behaviour cloning on demonstrations through Quadinaros, then trained further with RL in simulation on Anakin or Sebulba, with curricula over tasks through the same pit. The algorithms do not know they are driving a robot, just as they did not know they were writing tool calls.

How it compares

boonta stands on a lot of good work. PureJaxRL [Lu et al.] showed that compiling the whole loop into one program is the fastest way to do RL on accelerators. Stoix and Mava brought that to many algorithms and to cooperative multi-agent RL, PufferLib to very fast native environments, Cleanba to reproducible actor-learner training, and TorchRL to PyTorch. What boonta adds is mostly a matter of scope under one interface. It trains online, offline and through curricula with the same algorithm objects, runs on all three podracers, and treats pretrained LLMs and VLAs as just another torso. As far as I know it is the only JAX library that trains LLMs as agents this way.

What is next

The machinery is in place, and the next step is to use it for the question I actually care about, whether RL post-training teaches a model a skill or only fits its training tasks. boonta makes the ingredients of that question cheap to vary, the task distribution, the curriculum, the memory, the algorithm, and it makes held-out evaluation the default rather than an afterthought. If you want to try it, the quickstart trains PPO on Breakout one part at a time. And if you think one of the boundaries is in the wrong place, I would like to hear about it, so get in touch.

entry.title: Behavioral Language Modeling
entry.content:
I come to language models from RL, so I tend to think about a coding assistant as a policy. It reads a test failure, chooses a command, sees the result, and tries a patch. Some of the tokens in its context are decisions it made. Others came from the user or the terminal.

I’ve been working on behavioral language modeling, starting from the idea that pretraining on these interactions is imitation learning. That led me to compare learning the assistant’s behavior with predicting the whole transcript. I have some early results from that comparison below.

The policy view has also changed how I think about distillation and context compression. A teacher might know something the student has never seen. A summary might discard something the student will need later. In either case, predicting the teacher’s next token can be a poor guide to what the student should do.

Actions and observations

Suppose a coding assistant is trying to fix a failing test.

The assistant chooses the command and receives the test output. Its patch depends on both. We can write its policy as

\[h_t=(o_0,a_0,o_1,\ldots,a_{t-1},o_t), \qquad a_t\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid h_t).\]

Here \(a_t\) is one generated token, and \(t\) counts the agent’s token decisions. The observation \(o_t\) contains any input received since its previous token. While the agent is generating a response, no new input may arrive, so \(o_t\) can be empty. After a tool call, it can contain the tool’s reply. The history \(h_t\) includes all earlier observations and generated tokens. Instructions and observed rewards can be included in the observations too.

The assistant has not read every file or found the cause of the failure yet. It has to act with incomplete information. This is the setting of a partially observable Markov decision process, or POMDP [Kaelbling et al.].

The role follows who generated the token. Source code read from a file is an observation. The same code in a patch is a sequence of actions. Quoting an error message is also an action, since the assistant chose to emit it.

This depends on whose policy we are training. A model acting as a tool simulator would generate the tool replies instead.

For a single uninterrupted completion, the usual token MDP works well. The state is the prefix, the action is the next token, and the next state appends it. An MDP can also account for incoming tool results through its transitions. I use the POMDP view because I also want to think about what the agent has not seen and what it needs to remember.

A language model is a recurrent policy

The history in \(\pi_\theta(a_t\mid h_t)\) has to reach the network somehow. A recurrent policy maintains a memory of it

\[z_t=f_\theta(z_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_t), \qquad a_t\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid z_t).\]

The memory \(z_t\) carries information from earlier steps. In a GRU, it is a hidden state. A transformer can use a KV cache or recompute over its retained context. External notes and retrieved records can provide memory too.

For example, a Wordle agent generates a guess and receives feedback about its letters. Its next guess should use the feedback from all previous turns. A recurrent RL algorithm can train this policy whether a GRU or a language model processes the history.

A cache does not guarantee good memory. The model might fail to use information that is present, and truncation might remove information it needs later. Nor is a hidden state automatically a sufficient belief state. That would require it to preserve all the information needed to predict the hidden state of the task.

Choosing a cache, summary, or retrieval scheme changes what the policy can remember. HELM uses this connection directly, with a pretrained language model compressing history for an RL agent [Paischer et al.].

Pretraining is imitation

An autoregressive language model learns to predict the next token in a corpus

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CLM}} =-\mathbb E_{x\sim\mathcal D}\sum_t \log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).\]

Here \(t\) counts positions in the corpus text. If the prefix is the history and the next token is an action, this is behavioral cloning with a log loss. The model learns to continue text like the text in its training data [Foster et al.].

The authors in that corpus have different goals and levels of skill. An edited document also hides most of the decisions its author made while writing it, so the connection to imitation is clearest with recorded agent interactions.

For recorded agent interactions, we can identify the assistant’s generated tokens and train their likelihood given the preceding history

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BC}} =-\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\mathcal D}\sum_t \log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid h_t).\]

Here \(t\) counts generated tokens. The model predicts a command from the request, then predicts a patch from the history that now includes the test result. Generated reasoning, stop tokens, and tool-handoff tokens are actions too. Fixed headers added by the interface are context.

The test output can train the model through its use in predicting the patch, without being a prediction target itself. How far those gradients flow depends on which computations are frozen, cached, or detached in the implementation.

Learning to predict observations

Suppose we instead predict every next token in the recorded interaction. We now train on the request and tool output as well as the command and patch. The summed loss over the same target positions splits into two parts

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{CLM}} =\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BC}}+\mathcal L_{\mathrm{WM}}.\]

Here \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BC}}\) predicts the agent’s actions and \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{WM}}\) predicts observations given the preceding history. I call the second term the world-model loss.

Predicting a test result might teach the model how the program works. It also asks the model to predict details it may never need when choosing a patch. I wanted to find out whether that extra training helps.

We can choose its weight explicitly

\[\mathcal L=\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BC}}+\lambda\mathcal L_{\mathrm{WM}}.\]

The loss normalization matters as well. If we average over all tokens, a long tool output contributes more targets than a short command. Averaging each part separately gives a different weighting.

This world-model loss fits observations in the dataset. Using it to predict what would happen after an unrecorded action requires assumptions about how the data was collected.

What happened on AgentTrove

I ran this comparison on recorded AgentTrove interactions with randomly initialized Qwen3-style models of about 82M, 191M, and 504M parameters. Within each pair, the architecture, initialization seed, data order, and optimizer were held fixed. CLM predicts all valid next tokens. BLM predicts only the assistant’s outputs. Both models read the observations. Each loss is averaged over the tokens it scores.

I evaluated both models on the same held-out assistant tokens. The plot shows their average negative log probability, or action NLL, so lower is better. Its horizontal axis is an estimated FLOP budget.

BLM finishes with lower action NLL in the 82M and 191M runs. At 504M, CLM finishes slightly lower. With one seed at each size, I would not infer a crossover point from this.

There is a catch in the compute accounting. It charges the output head only at scored positions, giving BLM a lower estimated cost per input token. I used that estimate to set the budgets, so the BLM runs process more training positions. The implementation still computes dense outputs. The lower estimated cost is not a measured runtime saving.

Counted in training positions instead, CLM is ahead early in training, and the smaller BLM models reach their lower final loss only after more positions. That is a different comparison from holding data exposure fixed. Intermediate checkpoints also come from runs with different schedule horizons, so they are not separate shorter-budget runs.

The validation filter removes detected task-name overlap with training, but cannot guarantee disjoint tasks. These are also single-seed runs. I regard them as early results on action prediction.

I also tried the 504M models in a separate 20-task development terminal pilot. Neither solved a task. The action-prediction results alone cannot establish better task performance or better learning during RL.

Learning from reward

In RL, we evaluate the policy by what happens when it acts

\[J(\theta)=\mathbb E_{\tau\sim P^{\pi_\theta}} \left[\sum_t\gamma^t r_t\right].\]

For the coding assistant, reward might depend on whether its patch passes the tests. Imitation increases the likelihood of demonstrated actions. A policy gradient update uses returns or advantages to change the likelihood of actions taken during rollouts.

Both methods train \(\pi_\theta(a_t\mid h_t)\). The observations remain inputs to that policy. In a fixed environment, policy ratios compare the probabilities of the actions, since the environment terms cancel. A KL penalty likewise compares the policy’s choices.

Implications

DAgger and on-policy distillation bring supervision onto histories the student visits [Ross et al.; Agarwal et al.]. The teacher’s advice also needs to account for what the student can observe. A teacher that has seen the source file may write a patch immediately, while the student should read the file first. Copying that answer can teach it to skip gathering evidence. This information mismatch is studied in asymmetric imitation learning [Warrington et al.].

Context compression changes the policy’s available information too. A summary could drop the source code without changing the next command, then leave the assistant unable to write the patch later. Work such as Continuous Context Management studies memory updates in language agents [Hoy et al.]. I would judge those updates by whether the agent can still finish the task after repeated compression.

entry.title: remembering without a replay buffer
entry.content:
This is an accessible writeup of a paper I wrote with Aryaman Reddi, Carlo D’Eramo, and Jan Peters, Streaming Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability with Real-Time Recurrent Learning [Farr et al.], which won a best paper award at the RL in Big Worlds workshop at RLC. In one sentence: we teach a streaming RL agent to remember, without a replay buffer and without ever unrolling the network through time.

Streaming RL in one paragraph

Most deep RL keeps a big replay buffer and learns from random minibatches sampled out of it. Streaming RL throws that out. The agent sees each transition once, updates immediately with a batch size of one, and never stores or replays anything. It is much closer to how a natural agent actually learns: online, incrementally, from a single stream of experience. For a long time this simply did not work with deep networks, they were too unstable, but a recent line of work on streaming deep RL got it stable and competitive. The catch is that all of it assumed full observability: the current observation tells you everything you need to know.

The catch: memory

Real environments are partially observable. The current observation does not tell you the whole state, so to act well the agent has to remember. That means a recurrent network carrying a hidden state, and a recurrent network only learns if the gradient can travel back through time: to discover that something you saw twenty steps ago mattered, credit has to reach twenty steps back.

There are two standard ways to do that, and under streaming both break.

  1. Backprop through time (TBPTT). Unroll the network over a window of past steps and backpropagate through the unrolled graph. But streaming has no buffer and a batch size of one, so there is no stored window to unroll. The truncation collapses to a single step, TBPTT(1). The agent can only assign credit to the step immediately before, and anything older is invisible. Long-range memory is off the table.
  2. Real-time recurrent learning (RTRL). Instead of looking backward, carry the gradient forward. At every step you maintain how the current hidden state depends on the parameters, and update that online as new observations arrive. It is exact and needs no buffer, which fits streaming perfectly. The problem is cost: for an ordinary recurrent network this bookkeeping scales quadratically or worse in the hidden size, which is hopeless for anything deep.

So one method fits the streaming constraints but cannot see the past, and the other sees the past exactly but is too expensive to run.

The idea: make the recurrence diagonal

The way out is to change the architecture so that RTRL becomes cheap. If the recurrence is diagonal, each hidden unit feeds back only into itself, then the way the hidden state depends on any one parameter stays local and decoupled from the others. You no longer need a full sensitivity matrix; a single running trace per parameter is enough to keep the exact gradient up to date. That collapses RTRL from prohibitive to linear in the number of parameters, in both time and memory.

This is exactly what recurrent trace units (RTUs) provide [Elelimy et al.]. The hidden state follows a diagonal recurrence,

\[\boldsymbol{h}_t = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\, \boldsymbol{h}_{t-1} + \boldsymbol{W}\, \boldsymbol{x}_t,\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is diagonal and complex-valued, with entries \(\lambda_k = r_k(\cos\Omega_k + i\sin\Omega_k)\). Each hidden unit rotates and decays its own past, with magnitude \(r_k\) and angle \(\Omega_k\). Because \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) is diagonal, every unit has a single recurrent connection to itself, and that is what makes exact RTRL linear in the number of parameters rather than prohibitive.

If you have used eligibility traces in RL, this is the same idea pushed into the recurrent hidden state. A trace is a running summary of the past that you keep current online, so credit can reach back arbitrarily far without ever storing the past. RTUs let the hidden state itself act as that kind of trace.

The result is the best of both options: RTRL’s exact, buffer-free, forward-in-time credit assignment, at a cost you can actually pay.

Dropping it into streaming algorithms

The clean part is that none of the surrounding streaming machinery has to change. RTUs slot in as the network inside the existing streaming algorithms, for both discrete-action and continuous-control agents. The update stays batch-size-one, buffer-free, and online. You swap a feedforward or truncated-recurrent network for an RTU and let RTRL carry the memory.

Does it actually help?

Three settings, from a pure memory stress test to real control.

MemoryChain. A diagnostic where the agent has to carry information across a chain of length 2 up to 128 before it can be rewarded. It is nothing but memory. The streaming TBPTT(1) baselines, whether feedforward, GRU, or even an RTU trained with one-step truncation, all collapse as the chain grows, because one-step gradients cannot reach the cue. Exact RTRL sustains performance across the whole range. The lesson is sharp: it is not the architecture that saves you, it is the exact online credit assignment. An RTU with TBPTT(1) fails right alongside the others.

POPGym. On five partially observable tasks, the streaming agents are competitive with batched PPO, which gets a replay buffer and batched updates that ours never use.

Masked MuJoCo. On partially observable continuous control, where either the velocities or the positions are hidden and the agent has to reconstruct them from history, the streaming agent recovers a substantial fraction of batched performance, again with no buffer and no batches.
